Association of Patient Language and Crowding with Wait Times at an Academic Medical Center Emergency Department

Brandon W. Yan, MD, MPH1,2  , Elizabeth Kwan, MD3, Nader Najafi, MD, MAS1,4, Yumiko Abe Jones, MS1,4, Maximilian J. Pany, MD, PhD5,6, Robert M. Wachter, MD1, and Jahan Fahimi, MD, MPH2,3

1Department of Medicine, UCSF School of Medicine, San Francisco, CA, USA; 2Philip R. Lee Institute for Health Policy Studies, University of California San Francisco, San Francisco, CA, USA; 3Department of Emergency Medicine, UCSF School of Medicine, San Francisco, CA, USA; 4Data Core, Department of Medicine, UCSF School of Medicine, San Francisco, CA, USA; 5Department of Emergency Medicine, Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, MA, USA; 6Department of Emergency Medicine, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Boston, MA, USA

## ABSTRACT

BACKGROUND:  Emergency departments (ED) provide timely care for acute conditions and serve as a vital safety net. Longer ED wait times are associated with worse health outcomes, but differences in ED wait times by patient language remain understudied. OBJECTIVE:  Examine differences in ED wait times between English and non-English language patients and its association with ED crowding. DESIGN:  Retrospective cohort study of ED visits at an academic medical center in 2023 and 2024. PARTICIPANTS:  73,420 ED visits among adult patients not triaged to the highest acuity categories. MAIN MEASURES:  Wait times from triage to provider assignment by patient primary language were assessed via unadjusted analyses and generalized linear models adjusting for demographic, temporal, and system factors as well as patient comorbidities and chief complaint. Language was then interacted with ED census to assess for effect modification from ED crowding. Secondary outcomes were time from provider assignment to ED disposition and rates of left without being seen (LWBS). KEY RESULTS:  Patients with a primary non-English language waited on average 6.5 min (p < 0.001) or 8.4% longer than English-primary patients for an ED provider—a difference that persisted after statistical adjustment (6.6 min, p < 0.001). Cantonese, Spanish, Russian, and Toishanese language patients experienced statistically longer wait times than English language patients. With ED census, each 10 additional patients in the ED were associated with an adjusted 2.3 min (p = 0.02) longer differential wait time for non-English language patients. Despite these differences, rates of LWBS were significantly lower for non-English language patients in both unadjusted and adjusted analyses (p < 0.001). CONCLUSIONS:  Longer ED wait times for patients with a primary non-English language reflect a health inequity affecting a disadvantaged population. The degree of disparity widened as ED census increased. Health system and policy attention is needed to address ED crowding and other factors that could contribute to this disparity.

KEY WORDS:  emergency department; wait times; language; low english proficiency; crowding

## INTRODUCTION

More than 150 million emergency department (ED) visits occur annually in the USA.1 As a critical part of the safety net, EDs provide time-sensitive care for patients irrespective of ability to pay as mandated by federal law. Prolonged ED wait times have been associated with more adverse events, worse health outcomes, patient dissatisfaction, and patients leaving without being seen.2–6 Black, Hispanic, Asian, and Spanish language patients have been shown to wait longer than white patients, and there is evidence that white patients tend to be assigned higher patient acuity scores for similar complaints than Black and Hispanic patients.7–10

In the USA, over 25 million people have limited English proficiency (LEP), an important social determinant of health.11 LEP has been associated with less access to care, lower rates of preventive screening, less medical comprehension, and worse health outcomes.11–16 In the ED context, patients with a primary non-English language, used as a proxy for LEP in prior studies, often experience higher rates of diagnostic testing, hospital admission, and ED revisits.17–19 Little data exist on how ED wait times differ by patient language. In a recent study of one ED, non-English language patients waited longer to be roomed and to reach a disposition.19 The American College of Emergency Physicians recommends wait time to provider contact as the preferred metric, reflecting the importance of this clinically vulnerable period before formal assessment by a trained provider.20

To help illuminate factors that may contribute to disparities and guide potential interventions, we investigated how wait times to provider assignment vary by patient’s primary language in an academic medical center ED and whether

## METHODS

Our primary analysis compared wait times to provider assignment by patient primary language in the adult ED of the University of California San Francisco Medical Center in San Francisco, CA, a quaternary level academic hospital that houses a 39-bed adult ED with over 40,000 annual visits.22 Language was determined by patient self-report. We compared wait times for English and non-English language patients in aggregate and individually for languages that comprised at least 0.5% visits (less common languages grouped into a composite category). We analyzed whether differences in wait times were influenced by ED census, the total number of patients in the ED at a given time including patients waiting to be seen, undergoing evaluation, or admitted and boarding in the ED. In secondary analyses, we compared time to ED disposition and rates of patients leaving before being seen by a provider after triage, henceforth referred to “left without being seen” or LWBS. ED visit data in calendar years 2023 and 2024 were obtained from the medical center’s Epic Systems electronic health record (EHR). Patients under 18 years old were excluded because they were generally re-triaged to an affiliated pediatric ED. Visits flagged with a “code” (e.g., cardiopulmonary arrest, code stroke, ST-elevation myocardial infarction activation, code 3 ambulance arrivals) or assigned the highest acuity number were excluded, as these cases typically bypass the standard workflow and receive immediate medical attention. Patient acuity was captured using the Emergency Severity Index (ESI) levels 1–5, with 1 being the highest acuity and 5 the lowest.23 This ED designates some lower acuity (ESI 3–5) patients as “fast-track,” whereby their care is expedited in a separate wing of the ED. Visits without a provider assigned or with a provider assigned before triage completion were excluded.

*Figure 1 illustrates the typical ED flow for patients. Patients check in before undergoing triage (i.e., vital signs and initial screening are completed by a registered nurse). Ideally, patients are then roomed before a provider assigns themselves to their care. Due to capacity constraints and ED crowding, provider assignment often occurs before rooming and history-taking and exam occurs by transferring patients in and out of temporary exam spaces. Language interpretation is available via a virtual video or voice interpreter. Considering this workflow, ED “wait time” was defined as the interval between triage completion and when the first provider assigned themselves to the patient’s care irrespective of bed status. Provider assignment to a patient typically occurs via self-assignment at the discretion of the ED provider (attending or resident physician or advanced practice provider), who reviews the waiting list in the EHR and selects the next patient to see based on factors such as acuity, wait time, and chief complaint. Time to ED disposition was defined as the interval between provider assignment and logged disposition (e.g., discharge, admission, transfer).*

Statistical Analysis

Study sample characteristics for English versus non-English language patients were compared using chi-squared testing for proportions and two-sided t-test for means. In primary analysis comparing average wait times by patient language, we used the two-sided t-test in unadjusted analyses. Due to anticipated heteroscedasticity, non-negative values, and right-skew of ED wait time data, we used generalized linear models with gamma distribution, log link, and robust standard errors and computed predicted mean wait times for adjusted analyses, which controlled for day of the week, time of day (6-h increments), year, season, ESI acuity level, “fasttrack” status, ambulance mode of arrival, outpatient referral, patient sex and age, Elixhauser comorbidity index, and chief complaint. Elixhauser scores were calculated through a 1-year EHR lookback for relevant ICD-10 codes. Due to the large number and heterogeneity of chief complaints, adjustment for chief complaint was performed in separate analyses limited to the top 10 most common in the sample. We also identified the median ED census of the study sample and performed the primary adjusted regression with two cohorts stratified by the median census. In secondary analysis, we compared time to ED disposition from provider assignment by patient language using the method described above. Due to isolated observations with implausibly short or extended times to disposition, the analysis was performed on the 1 st to 99th percentile of times to disposition to mitigate the impact of measurement error. Second, we compared rates of LWBS between English and non-English language patients using generalized linear models for adjusted analyses as described above except with binomial distribution. Since many LWBS patients left before a provider was assigned, the cohort analyzed followed the above exclusion criteria minus the requirement for provider assignment. Three sensitivity analyses were performed. First, we repeated the primary analysis with clustered standard errors at the patient level as a robustness check for potential non-independence among visits from the same patient. Second, we combined dialects of Chinese into a composite Chinese category and compared wait times versus English. Third, to assess whether findings are sensitive to levels of acuity, we repeated the primary analysis interacting English and non-English language with ESI. This study was approved by the University of California, San Francisco Institutional Review Board. Statistical analyses were performed in R version 4.4.1 and STATA version 18.0. Statistical significance was set at the p < 0.05 level.

## RESULTS

A total of 73,420 ED visits met study criteria (see Appendix A for exclusions). Languages comprising at least 0.5% of visits were English, Cantonese Chinese, Spanish, Russian, Mandarin Chinese, Toishanese Chinese, and Vietnamese. Patients with a primary non-English language were more likely to be female, older, higher acuity, and more medically complex than their English-primary counterparts (Table 1). In unadjusted analysis, English language patients waited 77.2 min on average between triage completion and provider assignment versus 83.7 min on average for non-English language patients—a difference of 6.5 min (p < 0.001) or 8.4% longer. Compared to the English group, average wait times were higher for all non-English groups, although only differences for Cantonese, Spanish, Mandarin, and the composite other languages reached statistical significance (Table 2). Adjusted analyses identified differences in wait times for several languages (Table 2). ## DISCUSSION

We found that patients with a primary non-English language waited about 8% (6.6 min) longer than patients with a primary English language for ED providers to assume their care. This gap widened as ED census increased. The time between provider assignment and disposition also tended to be longer for non-English language patients, but this was

largely explained by other factors such as differences in age. Despite waiting longer to be seen, non-English language patients were significantly less likely to leave before being seen by a provider. The clinical significance of the 6.6 min wait time difference, while not specifically studied, should be interpreted in the appropriate context. First, the aggregate mean includes many groups (e.g., Toishanese with 17.6 min longer average adjusted wait for visits with common complaints) and individuals waiting much longer. Second, triage screens for those emergent conditions where minutes matter but is widely known to face inaccuracies including, in one study, undertriaging one-third of emergent neurologic and cardiovascular conditions, and disparities would further exacerbate delays in care.24 Third, irrespective of long-term impact on health outcomes, a systematic disparity in wait time is unjust and contributes to worse patient experience. Our study finds differences in wait times even after accounting for potentially appropriate reasons for some patients to be seen sooner than others such as acuity level (higher acuity ought to take priority), outpatient referral status (substantial work-up may already be completed), and ambulance arrival (to free up emergency medical services to respond to other calls for service).25 These factors themselves are subject to inequities such as known differences in mistriage rates into both higher and lower acuity categories by race and differential access to outpatient care.26

Our findings are consistent with and extend prior work. Whereas Wong-Castillo et al. 2025 found disparities in wait

time to ED rooming, we find time from triage completion to provider assignment to be another key operational step where disparate wait times are introduced and one that ought not be explained by longer triage due to interpreter usage.19 Disparate wait times to provider assignment suggest queue jumping, wherein a later-arriving patient of similar clinical profile to an earlier patient gets seen earlier, is occurring. Our and Wong-Castillo et al.’s findings suggest that queue jumping, previously identified to affect Spanish language patients at a different ED, extends to other contexts and languages as well.10,19 Furthermore, language’s intersections with race and ethnicity might explain some of the disparities in ED wait times previously shown to afflict racial and ethnic minority patients.8,10,27

Wait time differences varied by non-English languages. Cantonese, Spanish, Russian, and Toishanese language patients waited statistically longer than English language patients after adjustment, while no statistical difference was detected for Mandarin and Vietnamese language patients after adjustment. With a growing Hispanic-American population and Spanish being the primary language for 13% of Americans, disparities affecting Spanish language patients will only grow in impact.28,29 Variations in wait times by Chinese dialect also have important equity implications considering Cantonese and Toishanese language populations in the USA tend to have less educational attainment and lower health literacy than their Mandarin language counterparts.30–32 Patients with less common primary languages also waited longer on average, although much of the difference was statistically explained by differences in chief complaint composition. Our findings point to ED overcrowding as a key driver of the language disparity. Exacerbated during the COVID- 19 pandemic, the national ED boarding crisis, in which patients admitted to the hospital “board” in the ED due to lack of inpatient beds, has led to a normalization of “waiting room medicine,” in which ED patients unable to be properly roomed are evaluated and managed in makeshift spaces.33,34 Considering the additional time and resources needed to evaluate patients requiring an interpreter (e.g., interpreter access, longer history taking, greater difficulty with privacy), providers facing high patient loads might select for patients who speak their language for waiting room evaluations and defer other patients. Policy action is urgently needed to address boarding through such measures as building capacity, realigning financial incentives, and addressing workforce shortages.34

Provider factors and interpreter availability are also important considerations. Provider discretion in patient selection could introduce implicit bias, particularly during periods of overcrowding and high patient loads when racial bias among ED providers is known to increase.21 Non-English language patients may be selected against due to perceptions of longer clinical evaluations, which is supported by

data showing longer times to disposition although the difference narrowed after adjustment for potential confounding.19 Interpreter availability, known to facilitate patient satisfaction, quality of care, and better health outcomes,35 remains a frequent source of provider frustration, particularly with limited availability of less common languages. Developing unbiased EHR tools for assigning patients to providers, ensuring availability of interpreter services, and expanding the multilingual workforce could help mitigate these factors. Lower rates of LWBS among non-English language patients, despite overall longer wait times, underscores the ED’s importance for language diverse communities. While this study lacks data on patient reasons for leaving, non- English language patients face unique barriers to care, language access being just one, that might otherwise facilitate alternatives to the ED or navigation of the broader healthcare system. Indeed, LEP patients are less likely to have a usual source of care and more likely to forgo necessary care, which renders the ED more essential when health issues arise.36 Thus, what may seem like reassuringly lower LWBS rates among non-English language patients is likely to reflect vulnerabilities and limited options.

## Limitations

This study has limitations. Although provider assignment does not reflect when the patient is seen face-to-face, studying its timing fits the intent to study provider decisionmaking on patient selection. Other clinically relevant or provider-specific factors that explain observed differences in wait times by language may not be captured in our analysis. EHR data may contain inaccuracies, such as from case-specific deviations from the standard ED workflow or measurement error. ED census includes boarding patients, which are cared for by inpatient teams but still contribute to geospatial and nursing strain. Lack of data on provider language abilities precluded study on the effect of language concordance. The clinical significance of wait time differences was not assessed, although the link between longer wait times and worse outcomes has been well documented.2–6,37 Future study is needed on whether closing the disparities meaningfully improves health outcomes. Findings from a single center may not generalize to other practice settings, such as settings where provider assignment is non-discretionary (e.g., via unbiased algorithm), less crowding enables uniform patient rooming and evaluation, or absence of trainees eliminates learning potential (e.g., for medical students) as a consideration in patient selection.

## CONCLUSIONS

Longer ED wait times for patients with a primary non-English language reflect a healthcare inequity afflicting a disadvantaged and largely immigrant community. Considering

longer wait times are known to be associated with worse health outcomes, this disparity warrants attention to mitigate potential harm. We find evidence for ED crowding as an exacerbating factor for disparate wait times, underscoring broader concerns regarding the impacts of a worsening national ED boarding crisis. Policy and institutional actions alike are needed to build adequate population-level ED capacity and provide the infrastructure and training to facilitate equitable care for patients of diverse language backgrounds.
